# Classically integrable boundary conditions {#sec-boundary-conditions}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Write down the boundary action, the boundary potential and the boundary condition at real and imaginary coupling, and show that energy is conserved.
- Derive the conserved charges on the half-line from Sklyanin's double-row transfer matrix, generalized to an arbitrary anti-automorphism $\sigma$.
- Reduce the compatibility condition with $\sigma$ = transposition to a node-by-node equation, and read off the classification of integrable boundary conditions, including three corrections to the published table.
- Obtain the soliton-preserving boundary condition from $\sigma$ = Hermitian conjugation and recognize it as $\Theta P$-invariance.
- Translate between the boundary parameters of the literature and the book's $C_j$.
:::

On the whole line, affine Toda theory is integrable because its field equations are the flatness condition of the Lax connection (-@eq-lax-pair). On the half-line $x\le0$ translation invariance is gone, and with it momentum and, more generally, every combination $Q_s-Q_{-s}$ of the whole-line charges (@sec-half-line-kinematics). A boundary condition is called integrable if infinitely many combinations of the remaining charges survive. For sine-Gordon there is a two-parameter family of such conditions [@gz1994]. For every other affine Toda theory the conditions are rigid: apart from the Neumann condition, most boundary parameters are forced to be $\pm1$. This chapter derives that rigidity from Sklyanin's formalism, collects the classification, and adds two further classes, the soliton-preserving condition and dynamical boundaries.

Everything here is classical. The quantum counterparts are the reflection matrices of @sec-boundary-scattering and @sec-soliton-reflection. The classical solutions on the half-line, which link the two, are the subject of @sec-half-line-solitons.

## Boundary potentials and boundary conditions {#sec-boundary-potential}

The field lives on $x\le0$, with the boundary at $x=0$. The action is

$$
S=\int dt\,\Big[\int_{-\infty}^0\mathcal L\,dx-\mathcal B\big(\vec\phi(0,t)\big)\Big],\qquad
\partial_x\vec\phi\big|_{x=0}=-\nabla\mathcal B\big(\vec\phi(0,t)\big),
$$ {#eq-boundary-action}

where $\mathcal L$ is the bulk Lagrangian of @sec-lagrangians and the boundary condition follows from the boundary term of the variation, $\int dt\,\delta\vec\phi\cdot(\partial_x\vec\phi+\nabla\mathcal B)|_{x=0}$. The boundary potentials that turn out to be integrable are

$$
\mathcal B_{\rm real}=\frac{2m}{\beta^2}\sum_jC_j\sqrt{\frac{2n_j}{\vec\alpha_j^2}}\left(e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}-1\right),\qquad
\mathcal B_{\rm imag}=-\frac{2m}{\beta^2}\sum_jC_j\sqrt{\frac{2n_j}{\vec\alpha_j^2}}\left(e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}-1\right).
$$ {#eq-boundary-potential}

The second follows from the first by $\beta\to i\beta$, exactly as $V_{\rm imag}$ follows from $V_{\rm real}$ in (-@eq-imaginary-potential). The boundary conditions are

$$
\partial_x\vec\phi\big|_0=-\frac m\beta\sum_jC_j\sqrt{\frac{2n_j}{\vec\alpha_j^2}}\;\vec\alpha_j\,e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}\quad\text{(real)},\qquad
\partial_x\vec\phi\big|_0=\frac{im}\beta\sum_jC_j\sqrt{\frac{2n_j}{\vec\alpha_j^2}}\;\vec\alpha_j\,e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}\quad\text{(imaginary)}.
$$ {#eq-boundary-condition}

The boundary potential has one term for each node of the affine Dynkin diagram, with the exponential $e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}$, the square root of the bulk term. The complex numbers $C_j$ are the **boundary parameters**. Two values recur.

- **Neumann**, $C_j\equiv0$: $\partial_x\vec\phi|_0=0$.
- **Uniform**, $C_j\equiv+1$: the "$(+\cdots+)$" boundary of Delius and Gandenberger [@delius_gandenberger1999].

The normalization $\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}$ is not cosmetic. @sec-durham-classification shows that it is exactly what makes the integrability conditions node by node, with the same allowed values for every algebra. It agrees with Bowcock, Corrigan, Dorey and Rietdijk [@bcdr1995], whose $A_i$ is $2C_i\sqrt{2n_i/\vec\alpha_i^2}$ (@tbl-boundary-dictionary).

**Energy.** The energy on the half-line includes the boundary potential,

$$
E=\int_{-\infty}^0\Big(\tfrac12\dot{\vec\phi}^2+\tfrac12\vec\phi'^2+V\Big)dx+\mathcal B\big(\vec\phi(0,t)\big).
$$ {#eq-boundary-energy}

Differentiating, using the field equation and integrating by parts gives $\dot E=\dot{\vec\phi}(0,t)\cdot\big(\partial_x\vec\phi+\nabla\mathcal B\big)|_{x=0}$, which vanishes by (-@eq-boundary-action). Energy is conserved for every boundary potential (@exr-boundary-energy). Integrability is the much stronger requirement that infinitely many further charges are conserved. The constants $-1$ in (-@eq-boundary-potential) normalize $\mathcal B(0)=0$. They do not affect the boundary condition, but they fix the zero of the boundary energy, which matters when vacua are compared in @sec-real-coupling-vacua.

**Is $\vec\phi=0$ a solution?** The constant field $\vec\phi=0$ satisfies (-@eq-boundary-condition) if and only if $\sum_jC_j\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}\,\vec\alpha_j=0$. Since $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_j=0$ is the only linear relation among the affine simple roots, this happens for $a_n^{(1)}$ exactly when all $C_j$ are equal. For other algebras it happens rarely: none of the 32 sign choices $C_j=\pm1$ of $d_4^{(1)}$ admits $\vec\phi=0$ (checked in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`). No other constant field helps. A constant solution of the bulk equation has $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_je^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}=0$, so all $e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}$ are equal, and all $e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}$ agree up to signs. The boundary condition then needs $|C_j|\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}\propto n_j$, that is $|C_j|\propto\sqrt{n_j\vec\alpha_j^2}$, which is impossible with $|C_j|=1$ when the $n_j\vec\alpha_j^2$ differ, as they do for $d_n^{(1)}$. This holds at real and at imaginary coupling, so for $d_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge4$, these boundaries have no constant vacuum at all. Their ground state must be a non-constant static solution. For $a_n^{(1)}$ such solutions are constructed in @sec-real-coupling-vacua. For $d_n^{(1)}$ with $C\equiv+1$ the vacuum is a static kink, unique because the energy is convex (@prp-dn-uniform-vacuum). At imaginary coupling the vacua are the points $\frac{2\pi}\beta\Lambda_W^\vee$, and $\vec\phi=\frac{2\pi}\beta\vec\mu$ satisfies the boundary condition with parameters $C_j$ exactly when the field $\vec\phi=0$ satisfies it with parameters $C_je^{i\pi\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\mu}$. At imaginary coupling a coweight shift therefore changes the sign pattern of the $C_j$, a fact that @sec-images-boundary uses constantly.

## Sklyanin's formalism {#sec-sklyanin}

Sklyanin [-@sklyanin1988] showed how a Lax pair produces conserved charges on an interval, provided the boundary conditions are compatible with a matrix $K$. We follow the slight generalization of Delius [-@delius1998b], in which an anti-automorphism $\sigma$ replaces Sklyanin's inverse.

**The Lax components.** Write the flatness condition (-@eq-zero-curvature) as $[\partial_x+a_x,\partial_t+a_t]=0$, with $a_t=\frac12(A_++A_-)$ and $a_x=\frac12(A_+-A_-)$. From (-@eq-lax-pair),

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_t(\lambda)&=\frac\beta2\,\partial_x\vec\phi\cdot\vec H+\frac m2\sum_jc_j\,e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}\big(\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}-\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big),\\
a_x(\lambda)&=\frac\beta2\,\partial_t\vec\phi\cdot\vec H+\frac m2\sum_jc_j\,e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}\big(\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}+\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big),
\end{aligned}
\qquad c_j=\sqrt{n_j\vec\alpha_j^2/2}.
$$ {#eq-boundary-lax-at}

**Transfer matrices.** On an interval $[x_-,x_+]$ let $T(\lambda)$ be the parallel transport of $\partial_x+a_x$ from $x_-$ to $x_+$, so that $\partial_{x_+}T=-a_x(x_+)T$. Flatness gives

$$
\partial_tT(\lambda)=-a_t(\lambda;x_+)\,T(\lambda)+T(\lambda)\,a_t(\lambda;x_-).
$$

On a circle the two boundary terms cancel under the trace and $\operatorname{tr}T$ is conserved. On an interval they do not, and the remedy is to send the transport back along the interval. Let $\sigma$ be an involutive anti-automorphism of the Lie algebra, linear or antilinear, extended to the group by $\sigma(gh)=\sigma(h)\sigma(g)$. Sklyanin's choice is $\sigma(X)=-X$, so that $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$. Define the **double-row transfer matrix** and its trace,

$$
\mathcal T(\lambda)=T(\lambda)\,K_-(1/\lambda)\,\sigma\big(T(1/\lambda)\big),\qquad
\tau(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\big(K_+(\lambda)\,\mathcal T(\lambda)\big),
$$ {#eq-double-row}

with two matrices $K_\pm(\lambda)$ that do not depend on the fields. Read from the left, $\mathcal T$ transports from $x_-$ to $x_+$, reflects there, and transports back from $x_+$ to $x_-$; the return trip is $\sigma(T(1/\lambda))$, and $K_-(1/\lambda)$ sits where the two meet, at the end $x_-$ of the first transport.

::: {#prp-sklyanin}
**[Established]** [@sklyanin1988; @delius1998b]

(a) If the boundary conditions at the two ends imply

$$
K_+(\lambda)\,a_t(\lambda)+\sigma\big(a_t(1/\lambda)\big)K_+(\lambda)=0\quad\text{at }x_+,\qquad
K_-(\lambda)\,\sigma\big(a_t(\lambda)\big)+a_t(1/\lambda)\,K_-(\lambda)=0\quad\text{at }x_-,
$$ {#eq-boundary-compatibility}

then $\tau(\lambda)$ is conserved for every $\lambda$.

(b) If, in addition, $K_\pm$ satisfy the classical reflection equations, which for $K_+$ read

$$
0=\overset1K_+(\lambda_1)\overset2K_+(\lambda_2)\,r\big(\tfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\big)+r^{\sigma_1\sigma_2}\big(\tfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\big)\overset1K_+(\lambda_1)\overset2K_+(\lambda_2)
+\overset1K_+(\lambda_1)\,r^{\sigma_2}(\lambda_1\lambda_2)\overset2K_+(\lambda_2)+\overset2K_+(\lambda_2)\,r^{\sigma_1}\big(\tfrac1{\lambda_1\lambda_2}\big)\overset1K_+(\lambda_1),
$$ {#eq-classical-reflection}

and for $K_-$

$$
0=\overset1K_-(\lambda_1)\overset2K_-(\lambda_2)\,r^{\sigma_1\sigma_2}\big(\tfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\big)+r\big(\tfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\big)\overset1K_-(\lambda_1)\overset2K_-(\lambda_2)+\overset1K_-(\lambda_1)\,r^{\sigma_1}(\lambda_1\lambda_2)\overset2K_-(\lambda_2)+\overset2K_-(\lambda_2)\,r^{\sigma_2}\big(\tfrac1{\lambda_1\lambda_2}\big)\overset1K_-(\lambda_1),
$$

then $\{\tau(\lambda_1),\tau(\lambda_2)\}=0$: the conserved quantities are in involution. Here $\overset1X=X\otimes1$, $\overset2X=1\otimes X$, and $r^{\sigma_1}$ means $\sigma$ applied to the first tensor factor. In part (b) $\sigma$ is linear and $\{a_x(\lambda_1;x)\overset\otimes,a_x(\lambda_2;y)\}=\delta(x-y)[r(\lambda_1/\lambda_2),\overset1a_x+\overset2a_x]$, with $r(z)=\frac{\beta^2}{4(z^h-1)}\big[(z^h+1)\sum_aH_a\otimes H_a+2\sum_{\alpha>0}\tfrac{\vec\alpha^2}2(z^{{\rm ht}\alpha}E_\alpha\otimes E_{-\alpha}+z^{h-{\rm ht}\alpha}E_{-\alpha}\otimes E_\alpha)\big]$ [@delius1998b, (3.4)], which satisfies $r^{t_1t_2}(z)=-r(1/z)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Part (a) is a two-line computation, which we give in full. Write $\mu=1/\lambda$ and $T=T(\lambda)$, $T'=T(\mu)$. Since $\sigma$ reverses products, $\partial_t\sigma(T')=-\sigma(T')\,\sigma(a_t(\mu;x_+))+\sigma(a_t(\mu;x_-))\,\sigma(T')$. Hence

$$
\dot\tau=-\operatorname{tr}\Big(\big[K_+a_t(\lambda)+\sigma(a_t(\mu))K_+\big]_{x_+}T K_-(\mu)\sigma(T')\Big)
+\operatorname{tr}\Big(K_+T\big[a_t(\lambda)K_-(\mu)+K_-(\mu)\sigma(a_t(\mu))\big]_{x_-}\sigma(T')\Big),
$$

and both brackets vanish by (-@eq-boundary-compatibility) (the second with $\lambda\leftrightarrow\mu$). Part (b) follows from the bracket of $T$ and the Leibniz rule for linear $\sigma$ [@delius1998b, Prop. 1] (re-derived); no property of $r$ beyond that bracket is used. With $\partial_{x_+}T=-a_xT$ and the bracket of $a_x$ stated in (b), that bracket is $\{\overset1T,\overset2T\}=-[r,\overset1T\overset2T]$: the generator of the transport is $-a_x$, whose bracket has the opposite sign. The classical reflection equations are linear and homogeneous in $r$, so the overall sign of $r$ affects neither them nor the involution. It matters when $T$ is combined with matrices whose bracket is fixed independently, as at a defect (@prp-defect-involution). Equation (-@eq-classical-reflection) is his (2.7), and the $K_-$ equation is his (2.8). That the stated $r$ is the r-matrix of the canonical brackets of $a_x$, and that the involution follows from the bracket of $T$ alone, is checked numerically for $a_1^{(1)}$ and $a_2^{(1)}$ in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py` (which uses the opposite overall sign of $r$, with the same conclusion); the sign of the bracket of $T$ is checked in `textbook_code/defect_lax_rmatrix.py`.
:::

For the half-line, take $x_-\to-\infty$ and $K_-=1$; the fields decay to a vacuum at $-\infty$, where the second condition holds trivially. The generating function $\tau(\lambda)$ is expanded in powers of $\lambda$, as on the whole line (@sec-conserved-charges), and produces an infinite set of conserved local charges. Heuristically, they are the combinations of the whole-line charges $Q_s$ and $Q_{-s}$ that are even under the reflection $x\to-x$: a charge carried out of the half-line by a right-moving excitation must be brought back by a left-moving one.

The compatibility condition (-@eq-boundary-compatibility) is linear in $K$ and contains $\partial_x\vec\phi$ at the boundary. Substituting the boundary condition turns it into an algebraic condition on $\mathcal B$. This is the whole content of classical integrability on the half-line. The rest of the chapter solves it for three choices of $\sigma$: transposition (@sec-durham-classification), Hermitian conjugation (@sec-soliton-preserving), and transposition with a $K$ that depends on extra boundary degrees of freedom (@sec-dynamical-boundary).

## The integrable boundary conditions {#sec-durham-classification}

Take $\sigma$ to be transposition, $\sigma(E_{\pm\vec\alpha})=E_{\mp\vec\alpha}$, $\sigma(\vec H)=\vec H$. Then $\sigma(a_t(1/\lambda))=\frac\beta2\partial_x\vec\phi\cdot\vec H-\frac m2\sum_jc_je^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}(\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}-\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j})$. With $K=1$ the compatibility condition reduces to $\beta\,\partial_x\vec\phi\cdot\vec H=0$: **the Neumann condition is integrable.**

For other boundary conditions substitute (-@eq-boundary-condition). The key identity is

$$
\sqrt{\frac{2n_j}{\vec\alpha_j^2}}=\frac{2c_j}{\vec\alpha_j^2},
$$

so the boundary term $\frac\beta2\partial_x\vec\phi\cdot\vec H$ becomes $-\frac m2\sum_jc_je^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}\,C_j\frac{2\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec H}{\vec\alpha_j^2}$. Each node now contributes the same prefactor $c_je^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}$ to the Cartan part and to the step operators. For a field-independent $K$, the coefficients of the $r+1$ linearly independent functions $e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}$ must vanish separately, and the compatibility condition becomes, with $h_j=2\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec H/\vec\alpha_j^2$ the simple coroot,

$$
K(\lambda)\big(-C_jh_j+\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}-\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big)=\big(C_jh_j+\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}-\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big)K(\lambda)\qquad\text{for every node }j.
$$ {#eq-boundary-k-equation}

Two features make this equation useful.

- **It is node-local.** The Lax coefficients $c_j$ have cancelled. With any other normalization of $\mathcal B$, such as dropping $n_j$, the factors $c_j$ survive and couple the nodes; for $d_4^{(1)}$ (where $n_2=2$) one then finds no invertible $K$ for any choice of signs (checked in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`).
- **It does not see the root normalization.** The equation involves only the coroots $h_j$ and the Chevalley generators $E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j}$, with $[E_{\vec\alpha_j},E_{-\vec\alpha_j}]=h_j$ (@sec-lax-pair), and these do not change when all roots are rescaled. So the allowed $C_j$ are the same in every normalization of the roots, including the different normalizations of twisted roots in the literature, provided $\mathcal B$ carries the factors $\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}$.

Equation (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) is the condition (4.10) of Bowcock, Corrigan, Dorey and Rietdijk [@bcdr1995] with $B_i=2C_i$ and their $K$ equal to our $K^{-1}$. Its solutions were found in [@cdrs1994; @bcdr1995] by expanding $K(\lambda)$ in $\lambda$. The lowest orders give necessary conditions. We have solved (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) in full, in a faithful representation, for every algebra marked "checked" in @tbl-durham. Two symmetries reduce the work. If $K$ solves (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) for the $C_j$, then $K^{-1}$ solves it for the $-C_j$, and $DKD^{-1}$ with $D=e^{i\pi\vec\mu\cdot\vec H}$, $\vec\mu$ a coweight, solves it for the $(-1)^{\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\mu}C_j$. For a simply-laced algebra the coweight flips connect all sign patterns with the same value of $\prod_jC_j^{n_j}$, so only one pattern from each of the two classes $\prod_jC_j^{n_j}=\pm1$ needs checking (both reductions checked for $e_6^{(1)}$ in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`).

| algebra | integrable $C_j$ (besides Neumann $C\equiv0$) | status |
|---|---|---|
| $a_1^{(1)}$ | $C_0$, $C_1$ arbitrary complex numbers | checked |
| $a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge2$ | all $C_j=\pm1$, signs independent | checked ($a_2$, $a_3$) |
| $d_n^{(1)}$ | all $C_j=\pm1$ | checked ($d_4$) |
| $e_6^{(1)}$ | all $C_j=\pm1$ | checked (27) |
| $e_7^{(1)}$, $e_8^{(1)}$ | all $C_j=\pm1$ | unchecked |
| $b_n^{(1)}$ | long nodes $C_0,\dots,C_{n-1}=\pm1$; short end $C_n$ arbitrary | checked ($b_3$) |
| $c_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge3$ | all $\pm1$; or short nodes $C_1=\dots=C_{n-1}=0$ with long ends $C_0$, $C_n$ arbitrary | checked ($c_3$) |
| $c_2^{(1)}=b_2^{(1)}$ | ($c_2$ labels: long ends $0,2$, short middle node $1$, which is node $n=2$ of $b_2$) $C_0,C_2=\pm1$ with $C_1$ arbitrary; or $C_1=0$ with $C_0$, $C_2$ arbitrary | checked; **first branch new** |
| $g_2^{(1)}$ | **all $C_j=\pm1$ only** | checked; **corrects [@bcdr1995]** |
| $f_4^{(1)}$ | all $\pm1$; or $C_0,C_1,C_2=\pm1$ with short $C_3=C_4=0$ | checked (27 of $e_6$, folded) |

| $d_4^{(3)}$ | **all $\pm1$ only** | checked (27 of $e_6$, both faithful summands); **corrects [@bcdr1995]** |

: Classically integrable boundary conditions with a field-independent $K$ and $\sigma$ = transposition. "Checked" means that an invertible $K(\lambda)$ solving (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) exists exactly for the listed $C_j$, tested against nearby non-listed values (`textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`). Unchecked rows are quoted from Appendix D of [@bcdr1995]. {#tbl-durham}

::: {#prp-durham}
**[Numerical]** For the algebras marked "checked" in @tbl-durham, an invertible field-independent $K(\lambda)$ satisfying (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) exists if and only if the $C_j$ are as listed. The same holds at imaginary coupling, where (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) is unchanged (checked for $a_2^{(1)}$ and $d_4^{(1)}$). For the simply-laced algebras the "only if" direction is also the analytic result of [@bcdr1995], obtained from the order-$\lambda^2$ terms of $K$.
:::

Three entries differ from Appendix D of [@bcdr1995]. The conditions listed there come from the order-$\lambda^2$ terms of $K$ alone, so they are necessary but need not be sufficient.

- For $g_2^{(1)}$, Appendix D allows the short-root parameter to be arbitrary. The full equation (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) has no invertible solution unless it is $\pm1$.
- For $d_4^{(3)}$, Appendix D also allows $C_0=C_1=0$ with the long-root parameter arbitrary. The full equation has no invertible solution on this branch (not even for $C_2=\pm1$); only Neumann and all $\pm1$ survive.
- For $c_2^{(1)}=b_2^{(1)}$, Appendix D lists only the $c_n$ branch. Since the same algebra is also $b_2^{(1)}$, the $b_n$ rule applies too, and the full solve confirms both branches. Similarly, $a_3^{(2)}\cong d_3^{(2)}$ obeys the union of the $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ and $d_{n+1}^{(2)}$ rules.

Why are the $C_j$ so rigid? For each node separately, (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) is the sine-Gordon problem, which has a solution for any $C_j$. The constraints come from asking for one $K(\lambda)$ that serves all nodes at once: the step operators of neighbouring nodes do not commute, and consistency at order $\lambda^2$ already forces $C_j^2=1$ in the simply-laced cases [@bcdr1995]. Sine-Gordon escapes because its two nodes act in the same $sl_2$, and in the non-simply-laced cases some nodes escape as well, as the table shows.

**Dirichlet conditions.** For sine-Gordon the Dirichlet condition $\phi(0,t)=\phi_0$ is the limit $M_0\to\infty$ of the Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov boundary, and it is integrable for every $\phi_0$ (@sec-boundary-sine-gordon). For the other theories @tbl-durham does not allow all the $C_j$ to be sent to infinity together, although in the non-simply-laced cases some of them can be. So full Dirichlet conditions have to be examined directly. For the untwisted algebras @prp-no-dirichlet does this within Sklyanin's construction: no field-independent $K_+$ exists in any finite-dimensional evaluation representation without trivial summands. The proposition does not exclude other constructions, for example a $K_+$ that depends on the fields, or a representation that is not an evaluation representation. Corrigan remarked, without proof, that Dirichlet conditions are "not generally permitted" [@corrigan1996, sec. 4].

::: {#prp-no-dirichlet}
**[Theorem]** Let $\hat g=g^{(1)}\ne a_1^{(1)}$, and impose $\vec\phi(0,t)=\vec\phi_0$ on all components, at real coupling or, for complex fields, at imaginary coupling. For generic $\lambda$ no field-independent $K_+(\lambda)\ne0$ satisfies (-@eq-boundary-compatibility). This holds when $\sigma$ is the antipode or the transposition composed with any conjugation, in any finite-dimensional evaluation representation without trivial $g$-summands. At imaginary coupling no antilinear $\sigma$ works either.
:::

::: {.proof}
At $x=0$ only $\partial_x\vec\phi$ is free. The conjugation in $\sigma$ can be absorbed into $K_+$, and since $\rho(X)^{\rm T}=-\rho^*(X)$ both cases read $K_+\rho(a_t(\lambda))=\rho'(a_t(1/\lambda))K_+$, with $\rho'=\rho$ or $\rho^*$. The Cartan part makes $K_+$ map weight spaces to weight spaces of the same weight. The step terms of node $j$ shift weights by $\pm\vec\alpha_j$, and for $\hat g\ne a_1^{(1)}$ these $2(r+1)$ shifts are distinct, so each cancels by itself. The factor $c_je^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi_0/2}$ is common to both terms of a node and drops out, leaving $K_+\rho(E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j})=\lambda^{\mp2}\rho'(E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j})K_+$ for $j=0,\dots,r$. So $\operatorname{Im}K_+$ is invariant under $\rho'(g)$. In an evaluation representation $E_{\vec\alpha_0}$ acts as a multiple of $E_{-\vec\theta}$. Since $\operatorname{ht}\vec\theta=h-1$, $E_{-\vec\theta}$ is a nested commutator of $h-1$ generators $E_{-\vec\alpha_j}$ with $j\ge1$. Moving $K_+$ through this commutator gives the factor $\lambda^{2(h-1)}$, while node 0 gives $\lambda^{-2}$. Hence $(\lambda^{2h}-1)\rho'(E_{-\vec\theta})K_+=0$, and for $\lambda^{2h}\ne1$ the generator $E_{-\vec\theta}$ annihilates $\operatorname{Im}K_+$. The elements of $g$ that annihilate an invariant subspace form an ideal. This ideal contains $E_{-\vec\theta}\ne0$, so it is all of $g$, because $g$ is simple. Then $\operatorname{Im}K_+$ is a trivial submodule of $\rho'$, by complete reducibility a trivial summand, and $\rho'$ has none. So $K_+=0$.

For antilinear $\sigma$ the real and imaginary parts of $\partial_x\vec\phi$ are independent, and the Cartan part gives $K_+\rho(\vec H)=0$ and $\sigma(\vec H)K_+=0$. So $K_+$ vanishes off the zero-weight space of $\rho$, and its image lies in the zero-weight space of $\sigma(\vec H)$. On the zero-weight space each term $K_+\rho(E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j})$ vanishes, because $\rho(E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j})$ maps it to other weights. The remaining terms $\sigma(E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j})K_+$ shift the weight by distinct amounts, so each vanishes. The image of $K_+$ is then annihilated by all generators, and $K_+=0$ as before. Checked numerically in `textbook_code/boundary_dirichlet.py`:

- for $a_2^{(1)}$, $a_3^{(1)}$ and $a_4^{(1)}$ with all such $\sigma$, including compositions with the diagram automorphisms;
- in the adjoint, $\Lambda^2$ and $V\oplus\bar V$ representations, and in the vector representation of $d_4^{(1)}$;
- for sinh-Gordon, where a $K_+$ exists in every case.
:::

The method of [@cdrs1994] gives an independent check that uses no $K_+$. For $a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge2$, the lowest charges have spin $\pm2$, and no combination of them survives $\vec\phi(0,t)=\vec\phi_0$. The energy-like flux at $x=0$ is a nonzero cubic in $\partial_x\vec\phi(0)$, and the momentum-like flux is not a time derivative (`textbook_code/boundary_dirichlet.py`). Dirichlet conditions on part of the components can survive. If $M$ is an involutive symmetry of the affine Dynkin diagram, the image condition $\vec\phi(x)=M\vec\phi(-x)$ imposes Dirichlet on the $M$-odd components and Neumann on the $M$-even ones, and it is integrable by the method of images. Full Dirichlet would need $M=-1$, which is a diagram symmetry only for $a_1^{(1)}$.

A solution $K$ of (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) also solves (-@eq-classical-reflection) [@bcdr1995; @delius1998b]; checked numerically for $a_1^{(1)}$ (generic complex $C_0,C_1$) and $a_2^{(1)}$ (sign patterns) in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`. If the boundary condition at $x_-$ is the same equation $\partial_x\vec\phi=-\nabla\mathcal B_C$, then $K_-(\lambda)=K_C(-1/\lambda)$ solves the condition at $x_-$ and the $K_-$ equation, because $a_t^T(-1/\lambda)=a_t(\lambda)$. (Delius writes $a_t^t(-\lambda)=a_t(\lambda)$, a misprint.) For a left boundary with energy $+\mathcal B_C$, i.e. $\partial_x\vec\phi=+\nabla\mathcal B_C$, take $K_-=K_C(\lambda)^T\propto K_{-C}(-1/\lambda)$. The parameters at the two ends are independent.

**The dictionary.** The literature uses at least eight conventions for the boundary parameters. @tbl-boundary-dictionary translates them. All entries were derived by comparing boundary conditions term by term and are checked in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py` unless marked "by hand".

| source | their parameters | book $C_j$ |
|---|---|---|
| Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov [@gz1994] | $\mathcal B=-M_0\cos\frac{\beta_{\rm SG}}2(\phi-\phi_0)$, $\beta_{\rm SG}=\sqrt2\beta$, $m_0=2m$ | $C_0=\frac{\beta_{\rm SG}^2M_0}{4m_0}e^{i\beta_{\rm SG}\phi_0/2}$, $C_1=\frac{\beta_{\rm SG}^2M_0}{4m_0}e^{-i\beta_{\rm SG}\phi_0/2}$ ($\vec\alpha_1=\sqrt2$) |
| Saleur–Skorik–Warner [@ssw1995] | $(\zeta,\eta)$; field on $x\ge0$ | $C_0=\cosh(\zeta+i\eta)$, $C_1=\cosh(\zeta-i\eta)$ |
| Corrigan–Delius [@corrigan_delius1999] | $(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1)$ (sinh-Gordon) | $(C_0,C_1)=(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1)$ |
| Corrigan et al. [@cdrs1994; @cdr1995; @bcdr1995] | $A_i$ | $A_i=2C_i\sqrt{2n_i/\vec\alpha_i^2}$; their Lax $B_i=2C_i$ |
| Bowcock [@bowcock1998] | $A_i$ in $\partial_x\phi=\sum A_i\sqrt{n_i}\vec\alpha_ie^{\vec\alpha_i\cdot\phi/2}$ | $A_i=-C_i$ (by hand) |
| Delius [@delius1998a] | $\epsilon$, field $\phi_D=i\beta\vec\phi$ | $C_j\equiv-\epsilon$ ($a_n$, $c_n$ only); position $\xi_D=-\xi$ |
| Delius [@delius1998b] | $A_i$ | $A_i=-C_i$ |
| Delius–Gandenberger [@delius_gandenberger1999] | $C_i$ | $C_i$; "$(+\cdots+)$" is $C\equiv+1$ |
| Baseilhac–Delius–George [@bdg2002] | oscillator $(\hat p,\hat q)$ | $C_0=\cos\hat p$, $C_1=\cos\hat q$ |

: Boundary parameters in the literature and the book's $C_j$ of (-@eq-boundary-potential). {#tbl-boundary-dictionary}

In particular, $C\equiv+1$ is Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov's $M_0=4m_0/\beta_{\rm SG}^2$, $\phi_0=0$, the Saleur–Skorik–Warner point $(\zeta,\eta)=(0,0)$, and Delius's $\epsilon=-1$; the sine-Gordon Neumann point is $(\zeta,\eta)=(0,\pi/2)$. The $C_j$ are real exactly when $\phi_0\in\frac{2\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}}\mathbb Z$.

## Background-field boundary conditions {#sec-background-field}

The boundary conditions so far contain no time derivatives. With more than one field component, a boundary term linear in velocities is also possible,

$$
\mathcal L_{\rm bdy}=-\mathcal B(\vec\phi)+\tfrac12\,\phi_a\,b_{ab}\,\partial_t\phi_b,\qquad
\partial_x\phi_a\big|_0=b_{ab}\,\partial_t\phi_b-\partial_a\mathcal B,
$$

with $b_{ab}$ a constant antisymmetric matrix, the boundary value of a background two-form. The sign of the $b$-term follows from varying $\mathcal L_{\rm bdy}$: after an integration by parts in $t$, antisymmetry turns $\delta\big(\frac12\phi_ab_{ab}\dot\phi_b\big)$ into $\delta\phi_a\,b_{ab}\dot\phi_b$, which combines with $-\delta\phi_a\partial_x\phi_a$ from the bulk. Bowcock, Corrigan and Rietdijk [@bcr1996] analysed integrability in this setting. The constant term $K(0)$ must implement a symmetry of the extended Dynkin diagram that is an inner automorphism of odd order, which leaves only $a_r^{(1)}$ (with conditions on $r$) and $e_6^{(1)}$ as candidates; the solutions they find are discrete, with no free parameter beyond the bulk coupling. We do not use these conditions in what follows, and we have not checked them.

## A soliton-preserving boundary condition {#sec-soliton-preserving}

Every boundary condition of @tbl-durham turns an incoming soliton into an outgoing antisoliton (@sec-images-neumann). Delius [-@delius1998b] found a condition under which solitons come back as solitons, by changing $\sigma$.

Take $\sigma$ to be Hermitian conjugation, $\sigma(E_{\pm\vec\alpha})=E_{\mp\vec\alpha}$, $\sigma(\vec H)=\vec H$, extended antilinearly. It differs from transposition only in that coefficients are complex conjugated. At imaginary coupling, with $\lambda$ real,

$$
a_t(\lambda)+a_t(1/\lambda)^\dagger=-\beta\,\partial_x\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi\cdot\vec H+im\sum_jc_j\operatorname{Im}\big(e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}\big)\big(\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}-\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big).
$$

::: {#prp-soliton-preserving}
**[Theorem]** With $\sigma$ = Hermitian conjugation and $K_+=1$, the compatibility condition (-@eq-boundary-compatibility) holds at imaginary coupling if and only if

$$
\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0,t)\in\frac{2\pi}\beta\Lambda_W^\vee\ \ \text{(Dirichlet)},\qquad\partial_x\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi(0,t)=0\ \ \text{(Neumann)}.
$$ {#eq-soliton-preserving}

At real coupling the roles of the real and imaginary parts are exchanged. So $\tau(\lambda)$ is conserved, and $K_+=1$ solves the classical reflection equation. Since $\sigma$ is antilinear, part (b) of @prp-sklyanin does not apply as written, and the involution of the conserved charges is not proved here.
:::

::: {.proof}
The Cartan part of the display above vanishes iff $\partial_x\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi=0$. Since $\operatorname{Im}e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}=e^{-\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi/2}\sin\big(\frac\beta2\vec\alpha_j\cdot\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi\big)$, the step-operator parts vanish iff $\vec\alpha_j\cdot\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi\in\frac{2\pi}\beta\mathbb Z$ for every $j$, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi$ lies in $\frac{2\pi}\beta$ times the coweight lattice. That $K=1$ solves the reflection equation is shown in [@delius1998b] and below. The $a_2^{(1)}$ case, at both couplings, is checked symbolically in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`.
:::

For $K_+=1$ the reflection equation reduces to $r(z)+r^{t_1t_2}(1/z)=0$ and $r^{t_2}(w)+r^{t_1}(1/w)=0$, which hold for the Toda r-matrix at real spectral parameters, where $r$ is real (both follow from $r^{t_1t_2}(z)=-r(1/z)$; checked for $a_1^{(1)}$ and $a_2^{(1)}$ in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`). For antilinear $\sigma$ and complex fields the proof of @prp-sklyanin (b) does not apply as written, because the bracket of $T$ with $\bar T$ is not given by $r$; the reflection equation itself holds for $K_+=1$.

The condition has no free parameter. For sine-Gordon, where the physical field is real, it is the Dirichlet condition $\phi(0)\in\frac{2\pi}\beta\Lambda_W^\vee$ at a vacuum. For higher theories, where solitons are complex, it is the natural generalization of Dirichlet: Dirichlet on the real part, Neumann on the imaginary part. With $K_+\ne1$ the real part may also sit halfway between vacua.

::: {#prp-soliton-preserving-half}
**[Theorem]** Let $\vec\nu$ be a coweight. With $\sigma$ = Hermitian conjugation and $K_+=e^{i\pi\vec\nu\cdot\vec H}$, the compatibility condition (-@eq-boundary-compatibility) holds at imaginary coupling if

$$
\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0,t)\in\frac\pi\beta\vec\nu+\frac{2\pi}\beta\Lambda_W^\vee,\qquad\partial_x\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi(0,t)=0 .
$$ {#eq-soliton-preserving-half}

For $a_n^{(1)}$ in the defining representation, a field-independent $K_+$ compatible with Dirichlet on $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi$ and Neumann on $\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi$ exists only if $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0)\in\frac\pi\beta\Lambda_W^\vee$, and it is then a multiple of $e^{i\pi\vec\nu\cdot\vec H}$. Every constant diagonal $K_+$ solves (-@eq-classical-reflection) at real spectral parameters. As for $K_+=1$, the involution of the charges is not proved.
:::

::: {.proof}
The Cartan part of $K_+a_t(\lambda)+a_t(1/\lambda)^\dagger K_+$ is $\frac{i\beta}2[K_+,\partial_x\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi\cdot\vec H]-\frac\beta2\{K_+,\partial_x\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi\cdot\vec H\}$. At a Dirichlet boundary $\partial_x\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi$ is free, so $K_+$ commutes with $\vec H$. For $a_n^{(1)}$ in the defining representation it is then diagonal, $K_+=\operatorname{diag}(k_1,\dots,k_h)$, and the Neumann condition on $\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi$ removes the anticommutator. Write $w_j=e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi/2}$. Node $j$ links the basis vectors $v_j$ and $v_{j+1}$ (node 0 links $v_h$ and $v_1$), and its terms in $\lambda E_{\vec\alpha_j}$ and $\lambda^{-1}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}$ give $w_jk_j=\bar w_jk_{j+1}$ and $w_jk_{j+1}=\bar w_jk_j$. So a nonzero entry propagates around the cycle of nodes, all $k_i$ are nonzero, and $(\bar w_j/w_j)^2=1$. Since $\bar w_j/w_j=e^{-i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi}$, this means $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi\in\frac\pi\beta\Lambda_W^\vee$. With $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi=\frac\pi\beta\vec\nu$ modulo $\frac{2\pi}\beta\Lambda_W^\vee$, the ratios $k_{j+1}/k_j=(-1)^{\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\nu}$ fix $K_+$ up to a factor. Conversely, in any algebra $e^{i\pi\vec\nu\cdot\vec H}$ commutes with $\vec H$ and conjugates $E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j}$ into $(-1)^{\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\nu}E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j}=(\bar w_j/w_j)E_{\pm\vec\alpha_j}$, so the step terms cancel. A constant diagonal $K_+$ commutes with the terms $e_{ik}\otimes e_{ki}$ and $e_{ii}\otimes e_{kk}$ of $r$ and $r^{t_1t_2}$, and multiplies the matching terms of $r^{t_2}$ and $r^{t_1}$ by the same factor $k_ik_k$, so (-@eq-classical-reflection) reduces to the case $K_+=1$. All three statements are checked for $n\le3$ in `textbook_code/boundary_dirichlet.py`.
:::

**Half-solitons at the wall.** For $a_n^{(1)}$ the coweights modulo $2\Lambda_W^\vee$ label $2^n$ distinct boundaries, and $\vec\nu\in2\Lambda_W^\vee$ is (-@eq-soliton-preserving). In the other classes the boundary value is not a vacuum, and no constant field of finite energy satisfies the condition. When the class contains the topological charge of a single soliton, half of that soliton is a static solution. A soliton of species $b$ at rest with $\operatorname{Re}\xi=0$ satisfies $\vec\phi(x)+\overline{\vec\phi(-x)}=2\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0)$. Here $\frac\beta\pi\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0)$ is its topological charge, a weight of the $b$-th fundamental representation, and the real part of its energy on $x\le0$ is half the soliton mass. Each nontrivial class contains exactly one complementary pair of weights of fundamental representations, $\sum_{i\in S}\epsilon_i\in\Lambda_b$ and $\sum_{i\notin S}\epsilon_i\in\Lambda_{h-b}$ with $|S|=b$. The charges of species $h-b$ are the negatives of those of species $b$, so either both weights are single-soliton charges or neither is. If both are, they give two half-solitons of equal mass, whose vacua at $x\to-\infty$ differ by a soliton charge. This covers all three nontrivial classes of $a_2^{(1)}$. It misses the classes that contain no single-soliton charge (@sec-topological-charges): two of the seven nontrivial classes of $a_3^{(1)}$, represented by $\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2$ and $\epsilon_1+\epsilon_4$, five of fifteen for $a_4^{(1)}$, and twenty-one of thirty-one for $a_5^{(1)}$. The counts follow from an exact enumeration of the $h/\gcd(b,h)$ charges of a soliton of species $b$ (`textbook_code/halfline_consolidation_checks.py`). No static solution is known for these classes. For sine-Gordon the class of the fundamental coweight is Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov's Dirichlet boundary at the maximum of the potential, $\phi_0=\pi/\beta_{\rm SG}$, with $K_+\propto{\rm diag}(1,-1)$. Its two ground states are the half-kink and the half-antikink (@sec-boundary-sine-gordon). For a class represented by a single-soliton charge, scattering off a half-soliton can be constructed as a three-soliton image solution: the soliton, its $\Theta P$ mirror and the half-soliton (@sec-images-preserving). Along it $\tau(\lambda)$ is conserved with $K_+=e^{i\pi\vec\nu\cdot\vec H}$, and not with $K_+=1$ (checked for $a_1^{(1)}$, $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_3^{(1)}$ in `textbook_code/boundary_dirichlet.py`).

**Image form.** A field on the whole line obeys (-@eq-soliton-preserving) at $x=0$ if

$$
\vec\phi(x,t)=2\vec v-\overline{\vec\phi(-x,t)},\qquad \vec v\in\frac{2\pi}\beta\Lambda_W^\vee .
$$ {#eq-theta-p-reflection}

Indeed, at $x=0$ this gives $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0)=\vec v$, and differentiating gives $\partial_x\operatorname{Im}\vec\phi(0)=0$. Equation (-@eq-theta-p-reflection) says that $\vec\phi$ is invariant under $\Theta P$ composed with a reflection through the vacuum $\vec v$, where $P:x\to-x$ and $\Theta:\vec\phi\to-\bar{\vec\phi}$ (@sec-theta-classical). Delius writes the same condition as $\vec\phi(x)=-\overline{\vec\phi(-x)}-\frac{2\pi}\beta\vec\lambda$ with $\vec\lambda$ in the coweight lattice. At $x=0$ it gives $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi(0)=-\frac\pi\beta\vec\lambda$. This is (-@eq-soliton-preserving) only for $\vec\lambda\in2\Lambda_W^\vee$. For the other coweights it is (-@eq-soliton-preserving-half) with $\vec\nu=-\vec\lambda$, which is integrable with $K_+=e^{i\pi\vec\lambda\cdot\vec H}$ and not with $K_+=1$ (`textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`, `textbook_code/boundary_dirichlet.py`). The images built from (-@eq-theta-p-reflection) are the subject of @sec-images-preserving.

Why does $\sigma$ decide between conjugating and preserving? Heuristically, the charges conserved on the half-line are the combinations of $Q_s$ and $Q_{-s}$ selected by $\sigma$. With transposition, matching the charges of the incoming and outgoing objects requires an outgoing antisoliton; the extra complex conjugation in $\sigma=\dagger$ conjugates once more and restores the original species. At the level of asymptotic charges this can be made precise: if the conserved combinations are $I_s=Q_s+Q_{-s}$, an incoming soliton of species $a$ and rapidity $\theta$ and an outgoing one of species $b$ and rapidity $-\theta$ must have $q_s(a)=q_{-s}(b)$, and since $q_{-s}(b)=q_s(\bar b)$ this forces $b=\bar a$; an extra complex conjugation, as in $\sigma=\dagger$, forces $b=a$. What is missing is a proof that $\tau(\lambda)$ generates exactly these combinations, which would require the abelianization of the Lax connection in the presence of a boundary. @sec-half-line-solitons makes this concrete with the method of images. In the quantum theory the distinction reappears as the two forms of the reflection equation, soliton-preserving and soliton-conjugating (@sec-reflection-equation, @sec-preserving-conjugating).

## Dynamical boundaries {#sec-dynamical-boundary}

The parameters $C_j$ need not be constants. Baseilhac, Delius and George [@bdg2002] coupled the sine-Gordon field to a boundary degree of freedom, a non-linear oscillator with canonical variables $(\hat p,\hat q)$. In book variables its Hamiltonian is the imaginary-coupling boundary potential of $a_1^{(1)}$ with operator-valued parameters,

$$
H_{\rm osc}=-\frac{2m}{\beta^2}\Big(\cos\hat q\;e^{i\beta\phi(0)/\sqrt2}+\cos\hat p\;e^{-i\beta\phi(0)/\sqrt2}\Big),\qquad\{\hat p,\hat q\}=\frac{\beta_{\rm SG}^2}4=\frac{\beta^2}2,
$$ {#eq-boundary-oscillator}

i.e. $C_0=\cos\hat p$ and $C_1=\cos\hat q$ in (-@eq-boundary-potential), up to a constant. The total Hamiltonian $H_{\rm field}+H_{\rm osc}$ generates the sine-Gordon equation in the bulk, the boundary condition $\partial_x\phi(0)=-\partial H_{\rm osc}/\partial\phi(0)$, and the oscillator equations $\dot{\hat p}=-m\,e^{i\beta\phi(0)/\sqrt2}\sin\hat q$, $\dot{\hat q}=m\,e^{-i\beta\phi(0)/\sqrt2}\sin\hat p$ [@bdg2002, eqs. (7), (9), (10)]. These signs use the convention $\dot f=\{H,f\}$ of [@bdg2002]; with $\dot f=\{f,H\}$ they flip. The total energy is conserved (checked symbolically in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`).

Integrability follows from Sklyanin's formalism with a **dynamical** $K$-matrix: $K_+(\lambda)$ depends on $(\hat p,\hat q)$, and the classical reflection equation acquires a term from the Poisson brackets of the entries of $K_+$ among themselves. The compatibility condition is then imposed with the boundary condition and the oscillator equations of motion [@bdg2002]. We do not reproduce the construction; @sec-bsg-dynamical treats the model in detail. As $\hat p,\hat q$ are frozen at constant values, the $C_j$ become constants and the general Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov boundary is recovered. In the quantum theory the oscillator becomes a $q$-oscillator, and Baseilhac and Koizumi [@baseilhac_koizumi2003] constructed the corresponding dynamical reflection matrices.

Note that $H_{\rm osc}$ is complex, as Baseilhac, Delius and George point out. It is, however, $\Theta$-symmetric in the sense of the next section.

## The antilinear symmetry $\Theta$ on the half-line {#sec-boundary-theta}

In the bulk, $\Theta:\vec\phi\mapsto-\bar{\vec\phi}$ maps solutions to solutions because $\overline{V_{\rm imag}(\vec\phi)}=V_{\rm imag}(-\bar{\vec\phi})$ (@sec-theta-classical). This is the classical shadow of the antilinear symmetry of @sec-antilinear. On the half-line the same is needed of the boundary term.

::: {#prp-boundary-theta}
**[Theorem]** $\overline{\mathcal B_{\rm imag}(\vec\phi)}=\mathcal B_{\rm imag}(-\bar{\vec\phi})$ for all $\vec\phi$ if and only if all $C_j$ are real. In that case $\Theta$ maps solutions of the half-line theory to solutions, and the energy (-@eq-boundary-energy) of $\Theta\vec\phi$ is the complex conjugate of that of $\vec\phi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$\overline{\mathcal B_{\rm imag}(\vec\phi)}-\mathcal B_{\rm imag}(-\bar{\vec\phi})=-\frac{2m}{\beta^2}\sum_j(\bar C_j-C_j)\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}\,\big(e^{-i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\bar{\vec\phi}/2}-1\big)$, and the functions $e^{-i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\bar{\vec\phi}/2}-1$ are linearly independent. Conjugating the boundary condition (-@eq-boundary-condition) then shows that $-\bar{\vec\phi}$ satisfies it whenever $\vec\phi$ does; the bulk is as in @sec-theta-classical. (Checked symbolically for $a_2^{(1)}$ in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`.)
:::

So all the rigid boundary conditions $C_j\in\{0,\pm1\}$ of @tbl-durham are $\Theta$-symmetric, and so is the oscillator boundary (-@eq-boundary-oscillator): with $\hat p,\hat q$ conjugated along with $\vec\phi$, the equations of motion of the coupled system are mapped to themselves (by hand). The free parameters of $a_1^{(1)}$ and of the non-simply-laced cases break $\Theta$ unless they are real. For the physical, real sine-Gordon field, $\Theta$ is $\phi\to-\phi$. A Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov boundary is invariant under it exactly when $\phi_0\in\frac{2\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}}\mathbb Z$, the case of real $C_j$. For $\phi_0\in\frac\pi{\beta_{\rm SG}}+\frac{2\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}}\mathbb Z$ the parameters $C_0=-C_1$ are imaginary and @prp-boundary-theta fails, but the boundary is invariant under $\phi\to\frac{2\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}}-\phi$, which is $\Theta$ followed by a shift between vacua. All other $\phi_0$ break both.

The soliton-preserving condition fits the same pattern with parity included. Equation (-@eq-theta-p-reflection) says that the field is invariant under $\Theta P$, up to a vacuum shift. Thus the two classes of boundary conditions are distinguished by how they treat $\Theta$:

- $\sigma$ = transposition with real $C_j$: the boundary is $\Theta$-invariant, and images are parity images, which conjugate the species (@sec-images-neumann).
- $\sigma$ = Hermitian conjugation: the boundary condition itself is $\Theta P$-invariance, and images are $\Theta P$ images, which preserve the species (@sec-images-preserving).

As on the whole line (@prp-hirota-energy), solutions whose asymptotic data are mapped to themselves by the relevant antilinear map have real conserved charges. This is how the classical energy of a complex reflected soliton comes out real, and it is why the missing-charge problem of @sec-missing-charges reappears on the half-line in a new guise (@sec-boundary-missing-charges).

## Exercises {#sec-boundary-conditions-exercises}

::: {#exr-boundary-energy}
Show that the energy (-@eq-boundary-energy) is conserved for any boundary potential $\mathcal B$ when the boundary condition (-@eq-boundary-action) holds. What goes wrong if one drops $\mathcal B(\vec\phi(0))$ from $E$?
:::

::: {#exr-node-local}
Derive (-@eq-boundary-k-equation) from (-@eq-boundary-compatibility) and (-@eq-boundary-lax-at). Then repeat the calculation with $\mathcal B$ normalized by $\sqrt{2/\vec\alpha_j^2}$ instead of $\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}$, and show that the conditions no longer decouple node by node when some $n_j\ne1$.
:::

::: {#exr-sg-k-classical}
For $a_1^{(1)}$ in the two-dimensional representation, take $K(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}k_{11}&k_{12}\\k_{21}&k_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ and solve (-@eq-boundary-k-equation). Show that a solution exists for all complex $C_0$, $C_1$, and that it is diagonal only for Neumann. *Hint:* the two nodes have $h_1=-h_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and $E_{\vec\alpha_0}=E_{-\vec\alpha_1}$ up to normalization.
:::

::: {#exr-uniform-vacuum}
Show that $\vec\phi=0$ satisfies the uniform boundary condition $C_j\equiv\pm1$ of $a_n^{(1)}$, and that for $d_4^{(1)}$ no choice of signs allows $\vec\phi=0$. *Hint:* $\sum_j n_j\vec\alpha_j=0$ is the only linear relation.
:::

::: {#exr-soliton-preserving}
Derive (-@eq-soliton-preserving) from the display preceding @prp-soliton-preserving, and work out the real-coupling version. Show that (-@eq-theta-p-reflection) implies (-@eq-soliton-preserving).
:::

::: {#exr-gz-dictionary}
Starting from the Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov boundary potential $-M_0\cos\frac{\beta_{\rm SG}}2(\phi-\phi_0)$, derive the entries of @tbl-boundary-dictionary for $C_0$ and $C_1$. Which $(M_0,\phi_0)$ give the Neumann boundary? Which give $C\equiv-1$?
:::

::: {#exr-oscillator-energy}
Using $\{\hat p,\hat q\}=\beta^2/2$ and the convention $\dot f=\{H,f\}$ of [@bdg2002], write Hamilton's equations for $\hat p$ and $\hat q$ from (-@eq-boundary-oscillator), and show that $H_{\rm field}+H_{\rm osc}$ is conserved. Show that $(\vec\phi,\hat p,\hat q)\mapsto(-\bar\phi,\bar{\hat p},\bar{\hat q})$ maps solutions to solutions.
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-boundary-conditions-notes}

The algebraic framework of reflection equations goes back to Cherednik [-@cherednik1984] and Sklyanin [-@sklyanin1988], whose double-row transfer matrix is (-@eq-double-row) with $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$. Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov [-@gz1994] found the two-parameter integrable boundary of sine-Gordon, and Saleur, Skorik and Warner [-@ssw1995] parametrized it by $(\zeta,\eta)$. The Durham group derived the rigidity of the boundary conditions of the other affine Toda theories, first from low-spin charges [@cdrs1994; @cdr1995] and then from the Lax pair [@bcdr1995]; Bowcock, Corrigan and Rietdijk [-@bcr1996] added the background-field conditions. Delius [-@delius1998b] generalized Sklyanin's formalism to arbitrary anti-automorphisms and found the soliton-preserving condition. Baseilhac, Delius and George [-@bdg2002] introduced the boundary oscillator, and Baseilhac and Koizumi [-@baseilhac_koizumi2003] quantized it.

Corrections and clarifications to the sources made in this chapter:

- Appendix D of [@bcdr1995] allows the short-root parameter of $g_2^{(1)}$ to be arbitrary. Only $\pm1$ (or Neumann) admits an invertible $K$.
- Appendix D of [@bcdr1995] allows $C_0=C_1=0$ with the long-root parameter $C_2$ arbitrary for $d_4^{(3)}$. No invertible $K$ exists on this branch, for any $C_2$; only Neumann and all $\pm1$ are integrable.
- Appendix D of [@bcdr1995] lists only the $c_n$ branch for $c_2^{(1)}$. Since $c_2^{(1)}=b_2^{(1)}$, the $b_n$ branch ($C_0,C_2=\pm1$, $C_1$ arbitrary) is also integrable; likewise $d_3^{(2)}=a_3^{(2)}$ obeys the union of two rules.
- Appendix C of [@bcdr1995] normalizes $C_0$ of $a_2^{(2)}$ differently ($B_0=-\sqrt2C_0$); this is harmless. Their (1.4), $|A_i|=2\sqrt{n_i}$, is our $|C_i|=1$ via $A_i=2C_i\sqrt{2n_i/\vec\alpha_i^2}$.
- As Delius notes [@delius1998a, p. 9], the boundary condition (1.5) of [@delius1998a], with a single $\epsilon$ multiplying $\eta_i\vec\alpha_i$, is an integrable condition of @tbl-durham for $a_n^{(1)}$ and $c_n^{(1)}$, where $\eta_i\vec\alpha_i^2$ is the same for all nodes. It is also integrable for $a_{2n}^{(2)}$ and $d_{n+1}^{(2)}$, where the nodes with a different $\eta_i\vec\alpha_i^2$ carry free parameters. For $b_n^{(1)}$ ($n\ge3$), $d_n^{(1)}$, $e_n^{(1)}$, $f_4^{(1)}$, $g_2^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ ($n\ge3$), $e_6^{(2)}$ and $d_4^{(3)}$ the factor $\sqrt{2n_j/\vec\alpha_j^2}$ is required (checked for $b_3$, $d_4$, $g_2$, $a_{2,4,6}^{(2)}$, $d_3^{(2)}$ in `textbook_code/boundary_classical.py`).
- Equation (1.5) of [@delius1998b] is written for $\phi_D=i\beta\vec\phi$, so its "Dirichlet on $\operatorname{Im}\phi_D$" is Dirichlet on $\operatorname{Re}\vec\phi$. Its image form (1.4) allows every coweight, but (1.4) implies (1.5), and the proof with $K_+=1$ applies, only for $\vec\lambda\in2\Lambda_W^\vee$. For the other coweights (1.4) is integrable with $K_+=e^{i\pi\vec\lambda\cdot\vec H}$ (@prp-soliton-preserving-half), which also solves the paper's (5.1)–(5.2).
